newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China says permits for Taiwan ship links imminent.
newsitem.headline: China says permits for Taiwan ship links imminent.

text.p: China is hastily processing a batch of applications by Taiwan shippers eager to make the first direct crossings of the Taiwan strait since 1949, a senior mainland China transport official said on Friday.
"We are rushing the job and it will be completed soon," Cao Zhongxi of China's communications ministry told Taiwan reporters in Beijing in comments broadcast by Taiwan television.
Cao did not say how many applications were being reviewed or specify when the review would be complete.
Taiwan media, quoting unidentified mainland sources, have said the first approvals were due in early April, with direct sailings tipped to start with great fanfare as soon as April 8.
Taiwan reports on Friday said Beijing was expected soon to unveil a list of 11 Taiwan and mainland shippers allowed to pioneer the direct crossings.
Taiwan transport vice minister Mao Chi-Kuo, asked about how Taipei would treat mainland shippers, said no applications had yet been received but that they could be processed swiftly.
"Once the mainland shippers' applications have been approved by the mainland and sent to Kaohsiung port, we estimate Taiwan will need less than a week to process them," Mao said.

Mao's reference to processing in Taiwan's southern port of Kaohsiung appeared to indicate that Taipei was treating the issue as a low-key matter between two local ports so as to avoid dealing directly with China's arch rival communist government.
Taiwan's Republic of China government, exiled from the mainland after losing a civil war in 1949, has prohibited direct shipping and other direct links ever since.

Anticipating a breakthrough, Taiwan shippers have scrambled to prepare ships appropriate for the short 300 km (180 mile) voyage between the ports of Kaohsiung and Xiamen in southeastern Fujian province.
"We expect a result in two weeks," said M.S. Tsay, spokesman for Taiwan's Yangming Marine Transport Corp.
Yangming has earmarked two foreign-registered ships with capacity of 300 TEU (20-foot equivalent units) and tentatively plans two Kaohsiung-Xiamen round trips a week, executives said.
Most of Yangming's ships are larger than 1,000 TEU and unsuitable for Xiamen, they said.
Another top candidate for receiving a permit, Yong Yeou Navigation Co Ltd, has 10 small ships ready and could run up to eight round trips per week if demand merits.
"It only takes about 18 hours to sail from Kaohsiung to Xiamen, so we can make up to eight trips with our ships," Yong Yeou president Lin Yi-fu told Reuters by telephone.
Lin said Taiwan's shippers were focused on profitability -- not the prickly political issues that have kept Taiwan and China apart since 1949.
"What concerns us is whether the cargo volumes will be large enough for so many shippers to share," Lin said.
Politics could intervene, however, as Taiwan is expected to anger Beijing in late March by hosting a visit by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama.

"Direct links should start in April if everything runs smoothly, but China may hold up progress with the Dalai Lama visiting Taiwan soon and President Lee (Teng-hui) planning to visit Panama in September," said one Taiwan shipper.
